meta.title: Lexical Relationships & Register
meta.randomizationRule: Randomize question selection/order and answer-option order on every attempt; never reuse an exact attempt signature.
meta.alignment: TKT Module 1 — Describing language: Lexis — word groupings, lexical relationships and register

questions.stem: The words “large” and “big” have very similar meanings in many contexts.
questions.prompt: What lexical relationship do they illustrate?
questions.explanation: Synonyms are words with the same or very similar meanings in particular contexts.

questions.stem: Which pair contains synonyms?
questions.explanation: “Begin” and “start” can have very similar meanings.

questions.stem: A teacher asks learners to replace “happy” with a word that has a similar meaning.
questions.prompt: Which lexical concept is the teacher practising?
questions.explanation: The task asks learners to identify a word with a similar meaning.

questions.stem: Which word is closest in meaning to “assist”?
questions.explanation: “Assist” and “help” are synonyms in many contexts.

questions.stem: Why should teachers avoid telling learners that two synonyms are always interchangeable?
options: Because synonyms may differ in register, connotation or context
Because synonyms always have opposite meanings
Because synonyms must sound the same
questions.correctAnswer: Because synonyms may differ in register, connotation or context
questions.explanation: Synonyms often overlap in meaning but may differ in formality, connotation or typical use.

questions.stem: The words “easy” and “difficult” express opposite meanings.
questions.prompt: What lexical relationship do they illustrate?
questions.explanation: Antonyms are words with opposite or contrasting meanings.

questions.stem: Which pair contains antonyms?
questions.explanation: “Accept” and “refuse” express opposite meanings.

questions.stem: A teacher writes “polite” on the board and asks learners for a word with the opposite meaning.
questions.prompt: Which lexical concept is being practised?
questions.explanation: The task focuses on finding an opposite meaning.

questions.stem: Which word is an antonym of “temporary”?
questions.explanation: “Permanent” contrasts directly with “temporary”.

questions.stem: Which pair shows a clear oppositional relationship?
questions.explanation: “Legal” and “illegal” express opposite meanings.

questions.stem: fork – knife – spoon – plate
questions.prompt: What term describes this group of words?
questions.explanation: A lexical set is a group of words connected by topic, meaning or function.

questions.stem: Which group forms a lexical set?
questions.explanation: These words belong to the same topic area: transport.

questions.stem: A teacher presents “stove, fridge, sink, microwave” together.
questions.prompt: Why can these words be taught as a lexical set?
options: They belong to the same topic area
questions.correctAnswer: They belong to the same topic area
questions.explanation: The words are semantically grouped around the topic of kitchen appliances or equipment.

questions.stem: Which group is NOT a word family but can be treated as a lexical set?
questions.explanation: These words are related by topic rather than by a common root.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes a lexical set from a word family?
options: A lexical set groups words by topic or meaning; a word family groups words by a shared root
A lexical set contains only verbs; a word family contains only nouns
A lexical set contains opposites; a word family contains synonyms
questions.correctAnswer: A lexical set groups words by topic or meaning; a word family groups words by a shared root
questions.explanation: Lexical sets are semantic groupings, while word families are morphological groupings around a common root or base.

questions.stem: “see” and “sea” are pronounced the same but have different spellings and meanings.
questions.prompt: What lexical relationship do they illustrate?
questions.explanation: Homophones have the same pronunciation but different meanings and usually different spellings.

questions.stem: Which pair contains homophones?
questions.explanation: “Right” and “write” are pronounced the same but have different meanings and spellings.

questions.stem: A learner confuses “there” and “their” because they sound the same.
questions.explanation: “There” and “their” share the same pronunciation but differ in spelling and meaning.

questions.stem: Which pair is NOT a pair of homophones?
questions.explanation: “Book” and “look” rhyme but are not pronounced identically.

questions.stem: Which definition best describes homophones?
options: Words with the same pronunciation but different meanings
Words with the same root and related meanings
questions.correctAnswer: Words with the same pronunciation but different meanings
questions.explanation: Homophones share pronunciation but differ in meaning and often spelling.

questions.stem: English speakers commonly say “make a decision” rather than “do a decision”.
questions.explanation: Collocations are words that commonly occur together in natural language.

questions.stem: Which combination is a common English collocation?
questions.explanation: “Heavy rain” is a conventional and frequent combination in English.

questions.stem: Which verb commonly collocates with “homework”?
questions.explanation: English commonly uses the collocation “do homework”.

questions.stem: A learner says “strong coffee” and “powerful coffee”. Which expression is the more natural collocation?
questions.explanation: “Strong coffee” is a conventional English collocation.

questions.stem: Why is collocation knowledge important for learners?
options: It helps them produce more natural combinations of words
It helps them identify only prefixes and suffixes
It helps them distinguish words that sound the same
questions.correctAnswer: It helps them produce more natural combinations of words
questions.explanation: Knowing typical word combinations supports more natural and fluent language use.

questions.stem: Compare: “Could you possibly assist me?” and “Can you help me?”
questions.prompt: Which lexical concept is illustrated by the difference in level of formality?
questions.explanation: Register refers to language choices associated with factors such as formality, situation and audience.

questions.stem: Which expression is more formal?
options: I would be grateful if you could reply.
questions.correctAnswer: I would be grateful if you could reply.
questions.explanation: This expression uses a more formal register suitable for professional or formal communication.

questions.stem: A teacher explains that “kids” is more informal than “children”.
questions.prompt: What aspect of lexis is the teacher focusing on?
questions.explanation: The difference concerns level of formality and appropriacy in context.

questions.stem: Which expression is most appropriate in a formal report?
options: The results indicate a significant improvement.
questions.correctAnswer: The results indicate a significant improvement.
questions.explanation: Formal reports normally use neutral or formal language rather than conversational expressions.

questions.stem: Why is register important when teaching vocabulary?
options: Learners need to know when and with whom a word or expression is appropriate
Learners only need to know how a word is spelled
Register tells learners whether two words rhyme
questions.correctAnswer: Learners need to know when and with whom a word or expression is appropriate
questions.explanation: Vocabulary knowledge includes knowing whether a word is suitable for a particular audience, purpose and situation.

questions.stem: Which pair is closest in meaning?
questions.explanation: “Purchase” and “buy” are synonyms, although “purchase” is generally more formal.

questions.stem: The teacher asks learners to match “rapid” with “fast”.
questions.prompt: Which lexical relationship is being tested?
questions.explanation: “Rapid” and “fast” have similar meanings in many contexts.

questions.stem: Which statement about synonyms is most accurate?
options: They may share core meaning but differ in register or typical context
They must be interchangeable in every sentence
They must have identical spelling patterns
questions.correctAnswer: They may share core meaning but differ in register or typical context
questions.explanation: Synonymy is often partial rather than absolute; usage, connotation and register can differ.

questions.stem: Which word is a synonym of “require” in this sentence: “The task requires careful planning”?
questions.explanation: Here “require” and “need” have very similar meanings.

questions.stem: “Residence” and “home” can sometimes refer to the same place, but “residence” is usually more formal.
questions.explanation: Words may be semantically similar while differing in level of formality.

questions.stem: Which pair has opposite meanings?
questions.explanation: “Increase” and “decrease” express opposing meanings.

questions.stem: The opposite of “optional” is:
questions.explanation: “Optional” means not required; “compulsory” means required.

questions.stem: Which pair illustrates antonymy created through a prefix?
questions.explanation: The negative prefix “im-” creates an opposite meaning.

questions.stem: Which lexical relationship is illustrated by “formal / informal”?
questions.explanation: The two words contrast in meaning.

questions.stem: A vocabulary exercise asks candidates to match “maximum” with “minimum”.
questions.explanation: “Maximum” and “minimum” represent opposite ends of a scale.

questions.stem: Which group forms a lexical set connected with assessment?
questions.explanation: These words are linked by the topic of assessment.

questions.stem: The words “airport, passport, luggage, boarding pass” can be grouped together because they share:
questions.explanation: They form a lexical set connected with air travel.

questions.stem: Which set is based on semantic topic rather than morphology?
questions.explanation: These items belong to the topic of computing but do not share one morphological root.

questions.stem: A teacher organises vocabulary under the heading “Weather”: windy, cloudy, humid, stormy.
questions.explanation: The words are grouped by a shared topic or semantic field.

questions.stem: Which statement is true of lexical sets?
options: They help organise vocabulary according to semantic relationships or topic
Every word in the set must have the same root
Every word in the set must be the same part of speech
questions.correctAnswer: They help organise vocabulary according to semantic relationships or topic
questions.explanation: Lexical sets are semantic groupings and can contain different word classes and unrelated roots.

questions.stem: Which pair consists of homophones?
questions.explanation: “Weak” and “week” are pronounced the same but differ in spelling and meaning.

questions.stem: A listening activity asks learners to distinguish the intended meaning of /peə/ in context: “pair” or “pear”.
questions.explanation: “Pair” and “pear” share the same pronunciation but have different meanings.

questions.stem: Which pair is NOT homophonous in standard pronunciation?
questions.explanation: “Food” and “foot” have different vowel sounds.

questions.stem: Which definition is correct?
options: Homophones sound the same but have different meanings
Homophones are words that commonly occur together
questions.correctAnswer: Homophones sound the same but have different meanings
questions.explanation: Shared pronunciation is the defining feature of homophones.

questions.stem: Why can homophones create spelling difficulties?
options: The pronunciation alone may not show which spelling and meaning is intended
They always belong to different registers
questions.correctAnswer: The pronunciation alone may not show which spelling and meaning is intended
questions.explanation: Because homophones sound the same, context is often needed to choose the correct spelling and meaning.

questions.stem: Which combination is the most natural collocation?
questions.explanation: “Take an exam” is a standard collocation in many varieties of English.

questions.stem: Which adjective commonly collocates with “mistake”?
questions.explanation: “Serious mistake” is a conventional adjective + noun collocation.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains an unnatural collocation?
questions.explanation: English normally uses “make a decision”, not “perform a decision”.

questions.stem: “Highly effective” is an example of which type of lexical relationship?
questions.explanation: “Highly” commonly occurs with adjectives such as “effective”.

questions.stem: A learner knows the meaning of “decision” but repeatedly says “do a decision”. What knowledge is mainly missing?
questions.explanation: The learner needs to know which words typically combine with “decision”.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the most informal register?
options: The lesson achieved its stated objectives.
questions.explanation: “Awesome” in this context is conversational and informal.

questions.stem: Which expression would be most appropriate in a formal email to an examination centre?
options: I am writing to enquire about the test date.
questions.correctAnswer: I am writing to enquire about the test date.
questions.explanation: The wording is appropriately formal and professional.

questions.stem: A learner uses “gonna” in a formal academic presentation.
questions.prompt: What vocabulary issue is most relevant?
questions.explanation: “Gonna” is associated with informal spoken language and may be inappropriate in a formal academic context.

questions.stem: The difference between “depart” and “leave” can partly be described in terms of:
questions.explanation: “Depart” is generally more formal than “leave” in many contexts.

questions.stem: Which statement about register is most accurate?
options: Appropriate language choices depend on audience, purpose and situation
Formal language is always better than informal language
questions.correctAnswer: Appropriate language choices depend on audience, purpose and situation
questions.explanation: Register is about selecting language appropriate to context, including audience, purpose and degree of formality.

items.example: kids is more informal than children

matchingSets.instruction: Match each item with the lexical term it illustrates.
